question: In Canada's 2021 Census, does the finding that 29.3% of households contained one person mean that 29.3% of adults lived alone?
generated_answer: No. The Census of Population counts dwellings, not people. Data on households are used to estimate the number of people living alone. According to the census, there were 3.9 million households that contained one person, which represents 29.3% of all households. This does not mean that 29.3% of adults lived alone. One person could be living alone in a household, or one person could be living with family members. This is why the estimate of the proportion of Canadians who live alone is derived from data on persons, not on households. In 2021, 15.4% of adults aged 15 and over—about 4.4 million people—lived alone. This represents more than one-quarter (26.8%) of Canadians who were living alone, and is also based on information collected by the census. The data on persons living alone show that in 2021, the share of men and women who were living alone was comparable, with 15.3% of men and 15.5% of women living alone. The proportion of men who were living alone was 10.6% in 1981, and 15.3% in 2021. The share of women living alone rose from 12.4% in 1981 to 15.5% in 2021. While the proportion of men and women living alone has increased since 1981, there is a difference in the types of households that men and women who live alone are living in. In 2021, more than one-third (35.3%) of men living alone were living in a dwelling that was owned, compared with 28.9% of women. By contrast, 33.4% of women who were living alone were living in a dwelling that was rented, compared with 28.2% of men. In 2021, 67.7% of Canadians who were living alone were aged 45 and over, up from 58.7% in 1981. In 2021, 12.9% of Canadians aged 85 and over were living alone, up from 5.5% in 1981. Of the 4.4 million Canadians who were living alone in 2021, 2.6 million were women. Among women living alone, 47.9% were 55 years of age and over. Among men living alone, 46.8% were 55 years of age and over. The data on persons living alone also show that in 2021, more than one-third (35.9%) of Canadians who were living alone were widowed. This was up from 19.4% in 1981. The share of Canadians who were living alone and who were married or common-law spouses in a dissolved marriage was 10.3% in 2021, up from 3.2% in 1981. The share of Canadians who were living alone and who had never married or been in a common-law relationship was 26.7% in 2021, up from 17.7% in 1981. The share of Canadians who were living alone and who were divorced was 26.6% in 2021, up from 18.8% in 1981. In 2021, 29.5% of Canadians who were living alone had a degree in an occupation, up from 21.1% in 1981. This included 17.2% of men who were living alone and 35.4% of women who were living alone. The proportion of Canadians who were living alone and who had less than a high school diploma was 24.4% in 2021, up from 13.9% in 1981. This included 18.4% of men who were living alone and 26.3% of women who were living alone. The proportion of Canadians who were living alone and who were employed was 56.7% in 2021, up from 46.9% in 1981. This included 62.9% of men who were living alone and 51.1% of women who were living alone. The proportion of Canadians who were living alone and who were retired was 32.8% in 2021, down from 40.1% in 1981. This included 29.9% of men who were living alone
